title: Cheapest Fare With Few Layovers
statement:
There are n cities, numbered 0 to n − 1. Each flights[i] = [from, to, price] is a one-way flight.

Return the cheapest total price to get from src to dst with at most k layovers. A layover is a city you land in and leave again on the way, so k layovers means at most k + 1 flights. If no such trip exists, return -1.

examples.why: The cheapest trip overall is 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 for 150, but it has two layovers. With one layover allowed, 0 → 2 → 3 for 250 beats the direct 400.

City 2 is cheapest to reach through city 1 (20), but that path has already used a layover. Reaching city 2 directly for 50 is dearer, yet it leaves enough layovers for 2 → 3 → 4. Keeping only the cheapest way into each city misses this.
With no layovers you need a direct flight, and there is none.

constraints: No two flights share the same from and to; from ≠ to
hints: Plain Dijkstra finds the cheapest trip, but it may use too many flights. Why can't you just run Dijkstra and then check the number of flights on the answer?
The best way to reach a city depends on two things now: the price and how many flights you have used. A dearer arrival with fewer flights can be the one that matters later.

Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds: round i finds the cheapest price using at most i flights. Relax every flight from a copy of the previous round's prices, so one round can never chain two flights.

explain.intuition:
Plain Dijkstra keeps one number per city: the cheapest price to get there. With a flight limit that is not enough. In example 2, city 2 is cheapest to reach via city 1, but that route has already spent a layover, and the route that continues to city 4 in time needs the dearer, direct arrival at city 2. Dijkstra settles city 2 at 20 and never looks at the 50 arrival again. The state you need is (city, flights used), not just the city.

Bellman-Ford handles that state naturally. After round i, price[c] is the cheapest way to reach c using at most i flights. To compute round i + 1, try every flight u → v once, starting from round i's prices. Run k + 1 rounds and read price[dst]. The one trap is updating the array in place: then a price set earlier in the same round can be extended in that same round, and a single round may chain several flights. Always read from the previous round's copy.

Dijkstra can be rescued too, by making the heap entries (price, city, flights used) and allowing a city to be expanded again whenever it is reached with fewer flights than before.
steps: Set price[src] = 0 and every other price to infinity.
For every flight [u, v, p]: if price[u] + p < next[v], set next[v] = price[u] + p. Read from price, write to next.
Return price[dst], or -1 if it is still infinite.
pitfalls: Relaxing in place in Bellman-Ford. When flights are listed along a chain, as in example 1, one round can walk the whole chain and the limit is silently broken.
Running Dijkstra with a visited set on cities only. Example 2 shows the cheapest arrival is not always the useful one.
Off by one on the limit: k layovers means k + 1 flights, so k + 1 rounds.

complexity.time: O(k · F), where F is the number of flights

solutions.title: Try every route
solutions.idea: Depth-first search over all routes of at most k + 1 flights, keeping the cheapest that ends at dst. Prune routes already dearer than the best.

solutions.title: Bellman-Ford with k + 1 rounds
solutions.idea: Round i holds the cheapest price to every city using at most i flights. Each round relaxes every flight from a copy of the previous round.

solutions.title: Dijkstra on (city, flights used)
solutions.idea: Pop the cheapest (price, city, used) entry. A city is worth expanding again only if this entry used fewer flights than every earlier one, because then it can reach places the cheaper entry could not.
solutions.time: O(n · k · log(n · k) + F · k)

followups: Return the route itself, not only the price. What do you store per round?
The limit is on total travel time instead of on layovers. Which of the three solutions adapts most easily?
